card.name: Yowlah
card.tagline: A traditional martial dance of the UAE and Oman, simulating battle and victory.
card.profile: Yowlah, also known as Al-Ayyala, is a traditional martial dance originating from Bedouin war traditions in the United Arab Emirates and Oman. It involves rhythmic chanting, drum music, and the manipulation of sticks, swords, or dummy rifles to simulate battle scenes. The dance is performed at weddings, national festivals, and official ceremonies, serving as a symbol of tribal unity and national identity. It was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2014.
card.insight: On 26 November 2010, 285 participants from three different tribes performed the largest Yowlah dance in Fujairah to celebrate before the Crown Prince.

card.profile_long: The Yowlah, frequently referred to as Al-Ayyala, is a foundational martial performance art practiced across the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman. Historically, the dance emerged as a Bedouin war ritual, performed to celebrate victory after tribal conflicts or the successful return of pearl-diving expeditions. Today, it serves as a vital expression of national identity, performed during weddings, national holidays, state visits, and even football matches. The dance is characterized by its simulation of a battle scene, where performers embody the values of defense, solidarity, and triumph. In 2014, the art form was recognized by UNESCO as part of the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, a status intended to facilitate the transfer of skills and values between generations. The performance structure typically involves two rows of approximately twenty men facing one another. These men carry thin bamboo sticks, which represent spears or swords, though dummy rifles made of wood and metal or real weapons may also be used. Between these rows, musicians provide a rhythmic foundation using large and small drums, tambourines, brass cymbals, leather bagpipes, and flutes. The rows of men move their heads and sticks in synchronization with the drum rhythm while chanting poetic lyrics that glorify nomadic life and tribal virtues. In the United Arab Emirates, women often participate by standing at the front of the performance, engaging in the 'naash' ritual, which involves tossing their long hair from side to side as a gesture of gratitude for the protection offered by the male dancers. The melody of the accompanying music is noted for having seven tones in an irregular, repeated pattern, with the specific poetry varying depending on the occasion. The role of the lead performer is often inherited and carries the responsibility of training new participants. While the Yowlah is inclusive of all ages and social classes, regional variations exist, such as the Razfah, the Ardah, and the more rural al-wahabbiyya, which may exclude female participation. In modern contexts, the Yowlah has transitioned into the competitive sphere, notably through the Al Meydan reality series and the Shaikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Championship, which have helped elevate the dance's profile among younger generations.

sections.origins_and_history: The Yowlah originated as a Bedouin war dance performed after victory in tribal battles or successful pearl diving. It is a ritual of tribal unity and defense, now serving as a symbol of national heritage in the UAE and Oman.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performers form two rows facing each other. Men hop from foot to foot while holding bamboo sticks, swords, or dummy rifles. They move their heads and sticks in synchronization with the rhythm. Women stand at the front, tossing their hair from side to side in the naash ritual.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music features large and small drums, tambourines, brass cymbals, leather bagpipes, and flutes. The melody consists of seven tones in an irregular repeated pattern, accompanied by chanted poetry.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men typically wear the white dishdasha. Women wear traditional dresses. The dance is performed in open spaces during weddings, festivals, and official ceremonies.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed for weddings, national celebrations, state visits, and football matches. It signifies tribal unity, defense, solidarity, and victory.
sections.notable_figures: The lead performer is usually an inherited role responsible for training others.
sections.regional_variants: Variations include the Razfah, Ardah, al-harbiyya, and al-wahabbiyya, the latter of which is found in rural and coastal areas of Ras Al Khayma and Fujairah.
sections.lineage: Rooted in Bedouin martial traditions and tribal war rituals.

basic_steps: Stand in a row facing another row of performers.
Hop from one foot to the other in time with the drum rhythm.
Move head and stick/weapon in synchronization with the row.
Spin or throw the weapon (for advanced performers).
teaching.formation: Two rows of men facing each other, with musicians in the center.
teaching.level_notes: The lead performer role is inherited and involves training others.

claims.text: The yowlah is a weapon dance of the United Arab Emirates and Oman, traditionally performed during weddings, celebrations, and other events.
The yowlah originated as a Bedouin war dance where men would spin rifles after victory in a battle.
The yowlah is recorded (as al-ayyala) on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage Items of Humanity in November 2014.
The largest yowlah dance as of 2019 took place in Fujairah on 26 November 2010, with 285 participants.
The yowlah is performed by men who wear a white dishdasha and hop from one foot to the other while brandishing sticks.
In the United Arab Emirates, girls wearing traditional dresses stand at the front, tossing their long hair from side to side.
